target_customer: Pharmaceutical and biotech partners and federal funders (NIH, NIDA) who would back or license a stimulant use disorder medication; eventual payers would be patients and health systems
problem: There is no FDA approved medication for cocaine or methamphetamine use disorder. Earlier dopamine transporter drugs were themselves addictive, so the field largely abandoned the target.
business_model: Preclinical drug development funded by grants, aiming to license or partner with pharma
product_category: Small molecule therapeutics for substance use disorder

education: Wake Forest University, biology undergraduate degree
Wake Forest University School of Business, master of arts in management

technical_complexity.rationale: Novel atypical dopamine transporter inhibitors derived from modafinil analogs licensed from NIDA, needing preclinical screening, animal efficacy and eventually clinical trials. One analog (JJC8-091) was later noted to have low bioavailability and possible cardiac safety issues.

defensibility.rationale: Exclusive license to NIDA compounds gives a patent position, and drug approval is a high barrier, but the science was early and a single lead had developability problems.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows a large pharma building the same non-addictive dopamine transporter approach for stimulant use disorder; the field had mostly abandoned that target.

market_need_then: No FDA approved treatment for cocaine or methamphetamine use disorder (YC page). Federal funders (NIDA, NIH Blueprint) actively funded the area, with a Blueprint grant reported at a potential 3.3 million dollars over four years.

identity.logo: A logo exists (shown in a Triad press piece) but no source describes it

brand_strength.rationale: Only local North Carolina biotech press and a young leaders honor; no evidence the brand mattered to funders beyond the science. The camel case EncepHeal spelling is unusual and the name does not explain itself.

outcome_analysis: EncepHeal was founded in 2015 by Wake Forest graduate students after the NIH Neuro Startup Challenge and licensed non addictive modafinil derived compounds from NIDA. It lived mostly on grants (a 300,000 dollar SBIR Phase I in 2017, state money, and a 2020 NIH U44 award) and joined YC in Summer 2019. YC lists it as inactive and calls Lazarus a former CEO, but no source says when or why it stopped; the cause is not public, so no failure factors are assigned. Directories disagree on status and a 2021 debt entry appears only on an aggregator.
notes: No company website is listed on the YC page. The 2017 SBIR and state grant amounts come from a Wake Forest blog post surfaced in search snippets, and the 2020 amount from Grantome; the NCBiotech article returned HTTP 403 so the Blueprint grant (potential 3.3 million dollars over four years) is not recorded as a round. Aggregators disagree: VCBacked shows 150K total with a debt entry in July 2021 (single aggregator, unverified), Village shows 300K, Seedtable shows none. The Innovation Quarter profile (2018-02) says over 500,000 dollars in grants in the first nine months. Competitors: Craft lists only algorithmic similar companies; no dated rival found for stimulant use disorder.
